=== REQUIREMENTS.md ===
# Mine

Mine is a set of PWAs (Progressive Web Apps) to digitalize once personal or professional life.
The key idea is to save everything in a repo as markdown files. This can be calendar entries, diaries, markdowns extracted from voice recordings / pdfs / .. These .md files can easily be ported to new apps without a vendor lock-in are processed via an (AI) assistant to help you plan your day, keep track of tasks, remind you of memories a.k.a. a second brain.
To keep complexity to a minimum each use-case will have a separate folder. e.g. the calender PWA lives completely in a 'calendar' folder as does the zettelkasten and all the other apps. Each folder contains a 'sample' folder with samples how the markdowns shall look and a REQUIREMENTS.md to describe how the PWA works.

## Main PWA

The main app is a PWA in the root directory with tiles to call the other apps.
Each tile has the apps folder name at the bottom and the respective icon.svg above it.

### PWA Setup & GitHub Sync

#### Initialization (first run)
- User opens the main app URL (GitHub Pages) on the phone.
- User installs it via "Add to Home Screen" (iOS: Safari → Share; Android: Chrome menu).
- On first launch, the app shows a setup screen asking for:
  - GitHub owner, data repo, and branch
  - Fine-grained personal access token (only this repo, "Contents: read and write", with expiry)
- App checks the connection with a test request (GET repo); on failure it shows a clear error.
- Settings and token are stored locally (IndexedDB); the token is never logged or displayed.
- Service worker caches the app shell so the app opens offline.
- App loads the file list with SHAs via the Git Trees API (recursive) and fetches all
  Markdown files into the local cache.

### Sending data to GitHub
- User creates, edits, or moves an item (e.g. Kanban card to "Doing").
- Change is written to the local cache immediately (UI updates instantly) and added
  to a sync queue.
- Sync worker processes the queue in order:
  - Create/update: PUT to the Contents API with the file content in Base64
    (UTF-8 safe, so umlauts work), a commit message, and the current SHA for updates.
  - Delete: DELETE to the Contents API with SHA and commit message.
- On success: store the new SHA returned by GitHub and remove the item from the queue.
- On conflict (409/422, file changed elsewhere): reload the file, keep the remote
  version, notify the user, and never overwrite silently.
- On 401/403: pause sync and link the user to settings to renew the token.
- Offline: the queue persists; sync runs automatically when the app regains
  connectivity or is reopened.
- A sync indicator shows: in sync / pending / error.

=== calendar/REQUIREMENTS.md ===
# Calendar
 # Calendar

Calendar is a plugin to manage your calendar.

Features

## UI
- The UI consists of a navigation pane at the top and a big calendar window on the rest of the window.
- In the top pane are these widgets from left to right:
  - left/right button to move to the previous/next day/week/month/year (depending on current view)
  - the current day/week/month/year with a small downward arrow to indicate a dropdown. When clicked a calendar month view is show with all days in this dropdown view. The month is shown on the top left and on the top right is a left/right arrow to go to the previous/next month.  When the user clicks on the month in the extended view it switches to year. The year view has all the last 9 years (3x3).
  - A dropdown to select the view to be either day/week/month/year.
    - The year view shows all months and days. On the top of each month is a ['M','T','W','T','F','S','S'] column indicating the weekday. Each row is a new week. Current day is highlighted. The user can click on the day and a popup shows the entries on that day. If there is a calendar entry on that day the day has the background color of the entrys group. For multiple entries they are split. If a user disables a group via the group dropdown filter then it is not shown.
    - The month columns are the workdays starting from monday. Each row is a new week. When the user clicks on a day it opens a popup to create a new calendar entry.
      - The calendar entry popup has a top row to fill the title below it a button group in a row to select the type. All other field (see the sample folder) are below it. At the bottom of the popup is a 'discard' and a 'save' button.
    - The calendar entry items are show as rows per day field in the month overview, Sorted by the time they start. The 'task' items have a rectangular icon at the right to mark them done. A completed item has a done arrow in the rectangle. For a task just the date is set, not the time (which is 00:00:00 to 23:59:59 for this day)
    - The week view shows the workdays starting from monday. The rows is the time showing all 24h of the day.
    - The day view is like the week view but only for the specific day. It shows more details of the calendar entries.
  - A dropdown to filter the calendar groups (color). If a user double-clicks on the calendar group icons he can add descriptions to the colors.
  -

content.text:
I've read `REQUIREMENTS.md`, `calendar/REQUIREMENTS.md`, both samples, and the icon. Short answers before the grilling starts:

**Is it possible?** Yes — but only if you build it a specific way. Shared token/settings works because *same origin = same storage*. `https://you.github.io/mine/` and `https://you.github.io/mine/calendar/` are the same origin (path is irrelevant to storage), so IndexedDB is shared automatically, no message passing needed.

The trap: that only holds while it's **one installed PWA**. If you install the calendar separately as its own home-screen app, iOS gives each home-screen web app its own isolated storage container — the calendar would come up with no token. (Worth verifying on your actual phone, but I'd design around it.) So "subfolders" must mean *source layout + routes inside one installable app*, not N installable apps.

**Do the REQUIREMENTS make sense?** The sync chapter is solid and realistic — Trees API for listing, Contents API with Base64 for writes, SHA tracking, queue, conflict on 409/422. That's the right shape. What's broken or missing:

1. No code-repo/data-repo split stated. Pages site must be public; your diary must not be.
2. `alert: on-start, 15` — **no browser can schedule a local notification while closed.** Notification Triggers API doesn't exist anywhere; iOS has no Background Sync either. Reminders are not implementable as written.
3. "fetches *all* Markdown files into the local cache" — fine at 500 files, not at 20k, and it couples every app to every other app's data.
4. The two calendar samples disagree with each other: `start:` vs `date:`, `done: None` vs `done: false`. `None` isn't YAML (it's a string, not null).
5. `repeat: weekly` with one-file-per-event has no answer for "skip this Tuesday" or "move just this instance" — and no `until`.
6. Filenames `20260418-1.md` give no stable identity; renaming/moving a day breaks it.
7. Conflict rule "keep the remote version, notify" = silently throwing away what the user just typed.

Starting at the root of the tree, because almost everything else hangs off it:

options.label: One PWA, folders are routes (Recommended)

content.text:
Good — that also means the setup screen's "owner / repo / branch" is the data repo, and the token can be scoped to a repo that contains no code.

Now the schema branch. Your two samples imply one entry = one file, but the naming (`20260418-1.md`) has a concrete multi-device failure: the counter is assigned at creation, so your phone offline and your laptop offline both mint `-2` on the same day and collide when the queue drains.

Also relevant: the Trees API gives you **every path + SHA in one request**, with no file contents. So whatever you put in the *path* is queryable for free, and anything only in the frontmatter costs a download of every file.

questions.question: How should calendar entry files be named and foldered in the data repo?

options.label: Date in path + random id (Recommended)
options.description: Month view needs only the tree listing to know which days have entries, then downloads just that month. Collision-free offline. Cost: moving an entry to another date is a rename = DELETE + PUT (2 calls), since Contents API has no rename.
options.preview:
calendar/2026/04/
  2026-04-18-1400-k3f9.md
  2026-04-18-0000-p7qm.md
calendar/2026/05/
  2026-05-02-0900-x2bt.md

month view  -> tree listing only, 1 request
move entry  -> delete + create
id = 4 random chars, no counter

options.label: Date + slug + id in path
options.description: Same as above but keeps a human-readable title slug, so browsing the repo on github.com is pleasant. Cost: either you rename on every title edit (delete+create), or the filename silently drifts from the title.
options.preview:
calendar/2026/04/
  2026-04-18-1400-phoenix-sync-k3f9.md
  2026-04-18-trash-p7qm.md

nice in the GitHub UI
title edit -> rename, or stale slug

options.label: Flat id-only, date in frontmatter
options.description: Path never changes, so moving an entry or editing a title is a single PUT and never a rename. Cost: the tree listing tells you nothing — you must download and parse every entry to render any view, exactly the 'fetch all Markdown' clause in REQUIREMENTS.
options.preview:
calendar/
  01JAQ7X3K9F2.md
  01JAQ7Y1P4QM.md

move/retitle -> 1 PUT, no rename
any view     -> needs ALL files cached
scales badly past a few thousand

options.label: One file per day, entries inside
options.description: Fewest files. But both samples are single-entry documents with their own frontmatter, so this means a different format (a list of entries per file), and two devices editing different events on the same day now conflict on one SHA.
options.preview:
calendar/2026/04/2026-04-18.md
  (contains BOTH the sync and
   the trash entry)

conflicts on same-day edits
requires rewriting the sample format

content.text:
Now the entry schema. Your two samples contradict each other in five places, and one of them is a real correctness bug: `date: '2026-04-18T00:00:00Z'` for the trash task is 02:00 local time in Berlin — an all-day task stored as a UTC instant lands on the wrong day for anyone not on UTC, and breaks twice a year on DST.

Other cleanups: `None` is a YAML *string*, not null (parsers give you `"None"`); `duration` is derivable from start/end; `alert` mixes a keyword and an integer in one list; `done` is meaningless on an event.

questions.question: How should the entry frontmatter be unified across event and task?

options.label: iCal-style: start/end switch type (Recommended)
options.description: One key pair for both kinds. A bare date means all-day/floating (no timezone bug); a full timestamp with Z means a real instant. This is exactly how iCalendar's DATE vs DATE-TIME works, so export to .ics later is mechanical. Absent keys replace all the 'None' values.
options.preview:
# event
title: "Project Phoenix: Weekly Sync"
type: event
start: 2026-04-18T14:00:00Z
end:   2026-04-18T15:00:00Z
group: work
location: "Conf 3B"
alerts: [0, 15]   # min before, 0=start
participants: [jane@ex.com]

# task (all-day: bare dates)
title: "take out the trash"
type: task
start: 2026-04-18
done: false
group: home
alerts: [0]

rules: omit empty keys, never "None"
       no duration (= end - start)
       done only on type: task

options.label: Explicit allDay flag
options.description: Keep start/end always as full timestamps and add `allDay: true`. More explicit to read, but redundant — and you must remember to ignore the time portion whenever allDay is set, which is the classic place this bug comes back.
options.preview:
type: task
allDay: true
start: 2026-04-18T00:00:00+02:00
end:   2026-04-18T23:59:59+02:00

2 sources of truth for one fact

options.label: Local wall time + tz field
options.description: Store what a clock on the wall said, plus the zone: `start: 2026-04-18T16:00` / `tz: Europe/Berlin`. Correct for 'my 9am standup stays 9am when I fly', but every comparison needs a tz library, and the samples' Z form is thrown away.
options.preview:
start: 2026-04-18T16:00
end:   2026-04-18T17:00
tz: Europe/Berlin

needs Intl/tz math everywhere
right answer for travel, more code

content.text: One thing I pre-empted in that preview and should put to you explicitly — I wrote `group: work`, but your sample says `group: "red"` and `calendar/REQUIREMENTS.md` treats the color as the group ("add descriptions to the colors"). That matters because it decides what happens when you want red to become blue.

questions.question: Is a group identified by its color, or by a name that maps to a color?

options.label: Name + groups.md mapping (Recommended)
options.description: Entries carry a semantic name. One file in the data repo maps name → color + description, so recoloring or renaming a group is a single-file edit instead of rewriting every entry. Still markdown, so it fits the no-lock-in rule. Config syncs across devices for free.
options.preview:
entry:   group: work

calendar/groups.md
---
groups:
  work:   {color: "#c0392b",
           label: "Work"}
  home:   {color: "#27ae60",
           label: "Household"}
  health: {color: "#2980b9",
           label: "Sport & Doctor"}
---

recolor work -> edit 1 file
unknown group -> fallback grey
no limit on group count

options.label: Color is the identity (as in sample)
options.description: Keep `group: "red"` and store descriptions for each color in groups.md. Matches the current REQUIREMENTS wording and sample exactly. Cost: changing a color means rewriting every entry that used it, and you are capped at the colors you can name.
options.preview:
entry:   group: red

calendar/groups.md
---
red:   "Work"
green: "Household"
---

recolor -> rewrite every entry
"red" carries no meaning in the file

options.label: Name, config only on device
options.description: Entries carry a name; the name→color map lives in IndexedDB settings next to the token, nothing extra in the repo. Cost: colors and labels are per-device, so your phone and laptop disagree until you re-enter them.
options.preview:
entry:   group: work

IndexedDB settings:
  groups: {work: red, ...}

nothing added to data repo
phone / laptop drift apart

content.text: Recurrence is the one place where the decision we just made bites. `repeat: weekly` on a file at `calendar/2026/04/…` must render in May, June, 2028 — so "month view = tree listing for that month" stops being true the moment one recurring event exists. That needs fixing explicitly, not papering over.

options.label: Separate always-loaded repeat/ folder (Recommended)
options.description: Recurring entries leave the date tree and live in calendar/repeat/, which is small (tens of files) and always fully cached. A view = that month's folder + all repeat files expanded in memory. Skipping or moving one instance is an exceptions list plus an ordinary dated file.

content.text:
What would you like to clarify about the recurrence question? 

For context, the specific thing I'm trying to resolve is: a weekly task stored as one file dated 2026-04-18 has to show up in May, 2027, and beyond — so either the file lives outside the date folders (and gets expanded in memory at render time), or the app writes out one real file per occurrence. If something in the framing is off, or you had a different model in mind — say so and I'll re-ask.

message.content: Can we rename 'repeat' to 'recurrence' and use RRULE from the iCalendar standard, RFC 5545?

content.text:
Yes — that's strictly better, and it buys more than a rename:

- `recurrence: "FREQ=WEEKLY;BYDAY=SA;INTERVAL=1;UNTIL=20270101T000000Z"` — `UNTIL`, `COUNT`, `INTERVAL`, `BYDAY` all come for free instead of you inventing them.
- RFC 5545 already has the exception vocabulary, so my ad-hoc `except:` becomes **`exdate:`** (skipped occurrences) and you also get **`rdate:`** (extra one-off occurrences bolted onto a series).
- `DTSTART` is just our existing `start`, so nothing new. Combined with the DATE/DATE-TIME decision we already made, `.ics` export becomes close to a direct field copy.

One cost to name: RRULE expansion is not a thing you want to hand-write — `BYSETPOS`, `BYMONTHDAY=-1`, DST-crossing weeklies are where everyone gets it wrong. That means a dependency (`rrule.js`, ~50KB, vendored as a local ESM file so there's still no build step) or restricting yourself to a documented subset the app actually parses. I'd vendor the library and support full RRULE on read, while the UI only *writes* the common cases.

Schema is now:

```yaml
start: 2026-04-18          # = DTSTART
recurrence: "FREQ=WEEKLY;BYDAY=SA"
exdate: [2026-05-02]       # skip these
rdate:  [2026-05-04]       # plus these
```

That still leaves the storage question open — `FREQ=WEEKLY` with no `UNTIL` renders forever, so the file can't be found by walking the month folder it was created in:

options.label: Separate always-loaded recurring/ folder (Recommended)
options.description: Any entry with a recurrence rule leaves the date tree. That folder stays small (tens of files) and is always fully cached, so a view = that month's folder, plus every rule expanded in memory for the visible range. Adding a rule to an existing entry moves the file.

lastPrompt: Can we rename 'repeat' to 'recurrence' and use RRULE from the iCalendar standard, RFC 5545?

content.text:
Direct consequence to settle: your trash sample is a `task` with `done: false` *and* a weekly rule. One file can't hold "done" for each week.

Note that RFC 5545 already answers this too — an overriding occurrence carries `RECURRENCE-ID` pointing at the original slot — so this can reuse the exact mechanism we just picked for "move one instance" instead of inventing a second one:

questions.question: How is per-occurrence state (done, moved, retitled) recorded for a recurring entry?

options.label: Override file per touched occurrence (Recommended)
options.description: One concept covers done, moved, retitled and cancelled: a normal dated file in the month tree carrying recurrence-id (the RFC 5545 field) that points at the slot it replaces. Always a fresh path, so it can never conflict, even created offline on two devices. The rule file is never rewritten.
options.preview:
calendar/recurring/trash-p7qm.md
  start: 2026-04-18
  recurrence: "FREQ=WEEKLY;BYDAY=SA"

calendar/2026/04/
  2026-04-25-0000-ov1.md
    series: trash-p7qm
    recurrence-id: 2026-04-25
    done: true

  2026-05-02-0900-ov2.md
    series: trash-p7qm
    recurrence-id: 2026-05-02
    start: 2026-05-02T09:00:00Z
    # moved to a time

render: occurrence replaced if an
  override matches its date
never conflicts (new path each time)
52 small files/yr if ticked weekly

options.label: List of done dates in the rule file
options.description: The recurring file keeps `done: [2026-04-18, 2026-04-25, ...]`. Fewest files, and the state sits right next to the rule. Cost: every tick is a write to one mutable file, so it is the one place two devices can collide, and a conflict there risks the rule itself. The list grows forever.
options.preview:
calendar/recurring/trash-p7qm.md
  recurrence: "FREQ=WEEKLY;BYDAY=SA"
  done:
    - 2026-04-18
    - 2026-04-25
    - 2026-05-09

1 file, no extra paths
single SHA = conflict hotspot
520 entries after 10 years
moves still need a 2nd mechanism

options.label: Sidecar state file per series
options.description: Rule stays immutable in recurring/; a companion file holds the mutable per-occurrence state. Separates 'what I intend' from 'what happened', so the rule is safe. Cost: a second file per series to keep in sync, and still a per-series hotspot.

content.text:
Now the read path. `REQUIREMENTS.md` says "fetches **all** Markdown files into the local cache" — I pushed back on that earlier, but having costed it out I think the clause is closer to right than my objection was. A decade of calendar entries is ~3000 files × ~500 B ≈ 1.5 MB, so mirroring is cheaper than range logic. The real problem isn't the bytes, it's that per-file fetching means ~3000 HTTP requests on first run.

Two facts that shape this: `GET /repos/{o}/{r}/tarball/{branch}` returns the whole tree in **one** request and browsers now gunzip natively via `DecompressionStream('gzip')` (tar itself is ~40 lines to walk); and `GET /repos/{o}/{r}/commits/{branch}` with `If-None-Match` returns 304 and **doesn't count against your rate limit**, so "has anything changed?" is nearly free.

questions.question: What is the local cache / refresh model?

options.label: Per-app mirror, tarball bootstrap (Recommended)
options.description: First open of an app downloads the whole repo once as a tarball and keeps only that app's folder. Afterwards a cheap 304-guarded ref check, then a tree diff and per-file fetch of just what changed. Every date works offline, search is local and instant, no range logic anywhere.
options.preview:
first run (2 requests):
  GET /tarball/main   -> gunzip, walk
  GET /git/trees?recursive=1 (SHAs)
  keep calendar/** in IndexedDB

on open + on window focus:
  GET /commits/main  If-None-Match
    304 -> done, costs no quota
    200 -> GET tree, diff SHAs,
           fetch changed files only

mirrors per app folder you open
offline for all dates
~40 lines of tar reading

options.label: Per-app mirror, per-file bootstrap
options.description: Same mirror and same refresh, but the first run walks the tree and fetches each file individually. No tar code at all. Cost: one request per file on first run — fine today with 2 sample files, minutes-long and near the 5000/hr limit after a decade.
options.preview:
first run:
  GET /git/trees?recursive=1
  then 1 GET per .md file
     2 files   -> instant
  3000 files   -> ~3000 requests

simplest possible code
first run degrades over years
(could add tarball later)

options.label: Lazy by visible range
options.description: Only ever cache the month folders you actually open, plus recurring/. Smallest storage and fastest cold start regardless of history size. Cost: range-tracking logic in every view, jumping to an uncached month needs network, and cross-app search cannot work offline.

  + calendar/recurring/

content.text: Write path. One thing our own data model changed: with random-id filenames and override files, nearly every write is a **create at a fresh path**, which can't conflict. But moving an entry to another date is now a delete + create — and with the Contents API that's two separate commits, so a crash or an offline queue drain interrupted in between leaves the entry duplicated or vanished.

questions.question: Which GitHub write mechanism should the sync queue use?

options.label: Git Data API, one commit per drain (Recommended)
options.description: Build blobs, a tree and a commit, then update the ref with the expected old SHA. A whole queue drain — any number of files, creates and deletes together — lands as one atomic commit, so a move is never half-applied. Rejection means someone else pushed: re-pull and retry, which succeeds because your paths are distinct.
options.preview:
drain queue:
  POST /git/blobs      x N
  POST /git/trees      (base_tree)
  POST /git/commits
  PATCH /git/refs/heads/main
     expects old sha, no force

move = delete+create, 1 commit
4 + N requests per drain, not 2 per file
rejected -> re-pull, rebuild, retry
~80 lines more than Contents API

options.label: Contents API per file (as in REQUIREMENTS)
options.description: PUT with Base64 content and the file's SHA, DELETE with SHA. Exactly what REQUIREMENTS.md already specifies, and the simplest possible code. Cost: one commit per file, a move is two non-atomic commits, and a 20-entry offline backlog is 20 commits.

options.label: Contents API, but moves avoided by design
options.description: Keep the simple Contents API and remove the only operation that needs atomicity: make the path immutable after creation, so changing an entry's date is a frontmatter edit and the file stays in its original month folder. Cost: the path stops telling the truth about the date.
options.preview:
2026/04/2026-04-18-1400-k3f9.md
  start: 2026-05-02   # moved!

every write = 1 PUT, never a move
filename and real date diverge
browsing the repo misleads you

content.text:
Conflict policy. The Git Data API retry already handles "someone pushed unrelated files". The genuine conflict left is: the same entry edited on your laptop and on your phone since the last pull. Detect it by storing, with each queued change, the blob SHA it was based on, and comparing that to the remote path's blob SHA at drain time.

`REQUIREMENTS.md` currently says "keep the remote version, notify the user" — which does not overwrite silently, but does throw away what you just typed.

questions.question: When the same entry was genuinely edited in two places, what happens?

options.label: Keep both, local becomes a sibling file (Recommended)
options.description: Remote stays at the canonical path; your version is committed next to it as a .conflict file and shown in the UI with a 'keep mine / keep theirs / keep both' prompt. Nothing is ever lost, the leftover is plain markdown readable in any editor, and the queue drains cleanly instead of jamming.
options.preview:
remote wins the real path:
  2026/04/2026-04-18-1400-k3f9.md

yours is preserved beside it:
  2026/04/2026-04-18-1400-k3f9
          .conflict-20261118.md
    conflictOf: 2026-04-18-1400-k3f9

UI: banner + keep mine/theirs/both
unresolved conflicts are visible
  on every device, not stuck on one
~10 lines, loses nothing

options.label: Keep remote, discard local (as written)
options.description: Current REQUIREMENTS behaviour: reload the file, remote wins, tell the user. Simplest, and honest about what happened. Cost: the edit you just made on your phone is gone, and the notification arrives after the fact with nothing to recover from.

Noticeably nicer in the common case — ticking a task on one device while retitling on another. Cost: a merge routine plus a 3-way body diff, for a window that is minutes long on a single-user app.

content.text:
Now the feasibility gap I flagged at the start, since the schema has `alerts: [0, 15]` and that field is currently a promise the platform can't keep.

The hard facts: there is **no** way for a web app to schedule a local notification for later — Notification Triggers was an origin trial that never shipped. Web Push works (iOS 16.4+ for installed PWAs), but it requires something *awake* at alert time to send it, and Periodic Background Sync doesn't exist in Safari. So a real reminder needs a scheduler somewhere outside your phone — which collides with "the token only ever lives on the device".

One way out that fits your architecture with no hosting at all: a **GitHub Actions cron in the private data repo**. It already has the data, it can hold VAPID keys as repo secrets, and it costs nothing. Caveat: scheduled workflows on GitHub are routinely delayed 5–20 minutes, so "15 minutes before" can arrive at 3 minutes before.

questions.question: What do `alerts` actually do in v1?

options.label: Stored only, fire while app is open (Recommended)
options.description: Keep the field in the schema (it is valid VALARM data and exports to .ics), and fire a real Notification when the app happens to be open at the time. Honest about the platform, zero infrastructure, no secrets anywhere. Cost: you will miss alerts for anything you are not looking at.
options.preview:
alerts: [0, 15]   # stored, exported

app open  -> setTimeout + Notification
app closed -> nothing fires

also: "today / next up" list on
  the tile screen, so opening the
  app is the reminder

0 infra, 0 secrets, no backend
REQUIREMENTS must say so plainly

options.label: GitHub Actions cron sends Web Push
options.description: A workflow in the private data repo runs every 5–15 min, expands entries due soon (RRULE included) and pushes to your registered devices with VAPID keys held as repo secrets. No server to host, data never leaves your repos. Cost: GitHub cron drifts 5–20 min, so alert timing is approximate.

  secrets: VAPID_PRIVATE, ...
  subscriptions/<device>.json
     committed by the PWA

real push to a closed phone
timing drifts 5-20 min

content.text:
Token security. Worth noting one thing that's *not* an option: the OAuth device flow would avoid a hand-made PAT, but GitHub's `login/device/code` endpoints send no CORS headers, so browser JS can't call them without a proxy. A fine-grained PAT is the only no-backend path.

What's left is the at-rest posture — and it has a project-wide consequence, because the real threat to a browser-held token isn't theft of your phone, it's any injected script on your origin being able to read IndexedDB.

questions.question: How is the PAT protected at rest, and what does that imply for the app?

options.label: Plaintext IndexedDB + strict CSP, zero CDNs (Recommended)
options.description: The token is as safe as your unlocked device, and the XSS route is closed off by policy instead of by encryption: a locked-down CSP and every dependency vendored into /shared/vendor/ rather than loaded from a CDN. Also tracks the token's expiry and warns before it lapses.
options.preview:
stored: {owner, repo, branch,
         token, expiresAt}
in IndexedDB, plaintext

<meta http-equiv="Content-Security-
  Policy" content="default-src
  'self'; connect-src 'self'
  https://api.github.com
  https://codeload.github.com;
  script-src 'self'">

consequence: no cdnjs, no unpkg,
  no Google Fonts - vendor all
never log or render the token
warn 14 days before expiresAt

options.label: Encrypted with a passcode
options.description: Token sealed with AES-GCM under a PBKDF2 key from a passcode you type on every cold start. Protects against someone with your unlocked phone poking at devtools. Cost: a passcode prompt before any sync, and the key sits in memory while the app runs anyway, so XSS is barely slowed.
options.preview:
passcode -> PBKDF2 -> AES-GCM key
IndexedDB holds ciphertext only

prompt on every cold start
blocks nothing once app is open
marginal gain over device lock

options.label: Token per device, short expiry, easy rotation
options.description: Plaintext as in option 1, but each device gets its own PAT with a 30–90 day expiry, and the settings screen makes rotation a two-tap job. Limits the blast radius and the lifetime of any leak. Cost: you mint a new token every couple of months, per device.
options.preview:
phone:  pat_A  exp 2026-12-31
laptop: pat_B  exp 2026-12-31

revoke one device independently
leak expires on its own
manual rotation every 30-90 days

content.text: Service worker. This is where self-hosted PWAs most often rot: a cache-first SW serves your app from 2026 forever, and on iOS you can't easily force it. Also important: `api.github.com` and the tarball endpoint must be network-only — an SW that caches an API response will hand you a stale ETag and silently break sync.

questions.question: What caching and update strategy should the single root service worker use?

options.label: Precache shell, SWR, prompt to reload (Recommended)
options.description: Instant cold start offline, fresh code within one launch. A version constant names the cache; the new SW waits, the UI shows 'new version — reload', and skipWaiting runs on your tap so you are never upgraded mid-edit. GitHub API requests bypass the SW entirely.
options.preview:
const V = '2026-11-18.1';
install -> precache shell:
  /, /manifest.json, /shared/*.js,
  /calendar/, /calendar/app.js,
  icons, /shared/vendor/*

fetch:
  api.github.com | codeload
     -> fetch(), never cached
  same-origin -> cache, revalidate
     in background

new SW waiting -> banner
  'Update ready - reload'
  tap -> skipWaiting + reload

~40 lines, no staleness trap

options.label: Network-first, cache as fallback
options.description: Always try the network for app files and fall back to cache when offline. Can never be stale and needs no update prompt or version juggling at all. Cost: every launch waits on the network for the shell, so a weak signal means a slow start rather than an instant one.
options.preview:
fetch: try network
  ok      -> use + store
  fail    -> serve from cache

no versions, no prompt, no skipWaiting
~15 lines
slow launch on bad signal
(the common phone case)

options.label: Cache-first with manual version bump
options.description: Fastest possible launch, simplest mental model: serve from cache, only fetch on a cache miss, bump the version constant when you deploy. Cost: forget the bump and your phone runs last month's app indefinitely with no way to notice.
options.preview:
fetch: cache.match() || fetch()

fastest start
stale until you remember the bump
hard to recover from on iOS

The year view explicitly lists seven columns `['M','T','W','T','F','S','S']`, but the month and week views both say "the workdays starting from monday". content.text:
Now the biggest unexamined assumption in `calendar/REQUIREMENTS.md`: the UI it describes is desktop-shaped. Top pane with three dropdowns plus prev/next, a 7×6 month grid, and entry rows *inside* each day cell. On a phone a month cell is ~50 px wide and ~60 px tall; an entry row is ~12 px. "Click on a day to open the create popup" and "click an entry row to open it" become the same tap target, and neither is reliably hittable.

This matters more than usual here because the phone is the primary install target.

questions.question: How does the calendar UI adapt to phone width?

options.label: Responsive, day-sheet on tap (Recommended)
options.description: One codebase, breakpoint-driven. On a phone, month cells show group-coloured dots instead of text rows, and tapping a day opens a bottom sheet listing that day's entries with a + to add — so tap targets are never smaller than a finger. On desktop, empty cell = create, entry row = edit, exactly as written.
options.preview:
PHONE (month)
 Mo Tu We Th Fr Sa Su
     1  2  3  4  5  6
           **    *
  dots = group colours
 tap day -> bottom sheet:
   14:00 Phoenix Sync   >
   [ ] take out trash
   [ + add entry ]

DESKTOP (month)
 cell shows entry rows
 click empty cell -> create popup
 click row       -> edit popup

same files, CSS breakpoint
top pane collapses to
  [<] [April 2026 v] [=] on phone

options.label: Identical layout, scroll/zoom
options.description: Render the same desktop grid everywhere and let the phone scroll horizontally. Zero adaptive code and the views look consistent. Cost: entry rows are unreadable and untappable at phone width, which is the device you said you want to use.

The most usable phone calendar there is, and simple to build. Cost: no month overview on the go, and a view that exists on one device only.

content.text: Dependencies, which the CSP decision now constrains: no CDNs, so anything we use gets committed into `/shared/vendor/` and precached. Two parsers are in play — frontmatter YAML and RRULE expansion. Both are places where "it's only 80 lines" is how you get silent data corruption years later: YAML because you'll hand-edit these files in vim and expect real YAML to work, RRULE because `FREQ=MONTHLY;BYDAY=-1FR` and DST-crossing weeklies are genuinely hard.

questions.question: Which parsers get vendored, and which get hand-written?

options.label: Vendor js-yaml + rrule.js (Recommended)
options.description: Both parsers are battle-tested, pinned by hand in /shared/vendor/, precached once by the SW. Hand-edited files always parse, and full RRULE works on read even though the UI only writes the easy cases. Cost: ~120 KB of vendored code you update manually, which for files you intend to keep for decades is the right trade.
options.preview:
/shared/vendor/
  js-yaml.mjs    ~70KB  (pin 4.1.0)
  rrule.mjs      ~50KB  (pin 2.8.1)
  (serialize YAML ourselves:
   we control output, so writing
   is ~20 lines, no dumper needed)

precached once, offline forever
no CDN, CSP-clean
manual version pins in a
  VENDOR.md with source URLs

options.label: Vendor js-yaml, hand-roll RRULE subset
options.description: Real YAML, but RRULE support limited to what you actually write: FREQ daily/weekly/monthly/yearly, INTERVAL, BYDAY, UNTIL, COUNT — about 100 lines. Covers your trash task and standups. Cost: an .ics import or a hand-typed BYSETPOS rule renders wrong rather than failing loudly.
options.preview:
yaml: vendored
rrule: ~100 lines, documented subset

FREQ=WEEKLY;BYDAY=SA      ok
FREQ=MONTHLY;BYDAY=-1FR   no
FREQ=...;BYSETPOS=2       no

must reject unknown rules
  loudly, not silently

options.label: Hand-roll both, zero vendored code
options.description: Nothing in vendor/, smallest possible payload, every line yours. Cost: a hand-rolled YAML reader mishandles quoting, multiline scalars and flow maps — and groups.md already uses flow maps. Highest risk of corrupting data you cannot easily notice.
options.preview:
~180 lines of parsing you own

smallest bundle
breaks on legitimate YAML:
  multiline: |
  quoted: "a: b"
  anchors, flow maps
silent misreads = data loss

content.text:
Main app home screen. Two things to settle at once: a static host can't list directories, so the app list has to be declared somewhere; and in the reminders decision I leaned on "opening the app is the reminder", which only works if the root screen actually shows something.

One mechanical note: you already have to hand-maintain the SW precache list when you add an app, so the app list can be the single source of truth for both — a module service worker (`{type:'module'}`, Safari 16.4+) can `import { APPS }` from the same file the tile screen uses.

questions.question: What does the root screen show, and where is the app list declared?

options.label: Tiles + today's agenda via widget.js (Recommended)
options.description: shared/apps.js is the one list, imported by both the tile screen and the SW precache. Apps may optionally ship a widget.js exporting summary(); the root renders whatever comes back above the tiles. Calendar's shows today and the next entry, which is what makes opening the app function as your reminder.

options.label: Tiles only, dumb root
options.description: The root is a pure launcher: icon.svg plus folder name per tile, exactly as REQUIREMENTS says, with zero knowledge of any app's data. Least code and no coupling at all. Cost: nothing reminds you of anything until you tap into the calendar.
options.preview:
/shared/apps.js
  export const APPS = ['calendar'];

  [calendar]   [zettel]

no coupling, no widget contract
opening the app shows you nothing
reminder story gets weaker

options.label: Full dashboard with widget slots
options.description: Root becomes a configurable dashboard: every app declares widgets, you choose which appear and in what order, state persisted. Powerful once you have five apps. Cost: a layout engine and a settings UI for one app that exists today.
options.preview:
widgets: [calendar.today,
          calendar.week,
          zettel.recent]
drag to reorder, show/hide
persisted per device

for 1 existing app

content.text: One field your popup spec never mentions, though both samples have one: the markdown **body** (the agenda text, the checklist). For a "second brain" that's where the actual content lives.

questions.question: How is the markdown body of an entry edited and displayed?

options.label: Raw textarea, raw display (Recommended)
options.description: An auto-growing monospace textarea at the bottom of the popup, below the frontmatter fields; display shows the same text with whitespace preserved. No renderer, no dependency, and what you see is exactly what lands in the file. Cost: checklists and headings look like markdown source rather than formatted text.

content.text:
Last branch. Before writing anything down, one risk I should name rather than bury: `GET /repos/{o}/{r}/tarball/{ref}` 302-redirects to `codeload.github.com`, and I'm not certain codeload sends `Access-Control-Allow-Origin` for authenticated private-repo downloads. If it doesn't, the tarball bootstrap fails in the browser and falls back to per-file fetching. That's a 20-minute spike, and it's the only decision above that could be invalidated by reality.

Two other unverified assumptions worth the same treatment: that an installed iOS PWA at `/mine/` really does share IndexedDB across `/mine/calendar/`, and that `{type:'module'}` service workers work on your iOS version.

questions.question: What should I do next?

options.label: Rewrite both REQUIREMENTS.md now (Recommended)
options.description: Capture all 14 decisions in the two requirements files, with the three unverified assumptions marked explicitly as spikes plus their documented fallbacks. You asked whether the docs make sense — this makes them make sense, and the spikes can only change one clause each.
options.preview:
/REQUIREMENTS.md
  + code repo / data repo split
  + one PWA, folders as routes
  + tarball bootstrap + ref guard

cat > REQUIREMENTS.md <<'EOF'
# Mine

Mine is a set of PWAs (Progressive Web Apps) to digitalize ones personal or professional life.
The key idea is to save everything in a repo as markdown files. This can be calendar entries, diaries, markdowns extracted from voice recordings / pdfs / .. These .md files can easily be ported to new apps without a vendor lock-in and are processed via an (AI) assistant to help you plan your day, keep track of tasks, remind you of memories a.k.a. a second brain.
To keep complexity to a minimum each use-case lives in a separate folder. e.g. the calendar PWA lives completely in a 'calendar' folder as does the zettelkasten and all the other apps. Each folder contains a 'sample' folder with samples how the markdowns shall look and a REQUIREMENTS.md to describe how the PWA works.

## Two repositories

| Repo | Visibility | Contents |
| --- | --- | --- |
| `maximilianharr/mine` | public | this app, served by GitHub Pages at `/mine/` |
| `maximilianharr/mine-data` | **private** | the markdown data: `calendar/`, `zettelkasten/`, ... |

The app repo must be public because GitHub Pages cannot serve a private repo without
GitHub Enterprise. Data therefore never lives in this repo — it would be world-readable
at a predictable URL. The token the app holds is scoped to the data repo only, so a
leaked token cannot modify the app itself.

## One installable app, folders are routes

Mine is **one** PWA, not one PWA per folder. There is a single `manifest.json` with
`scope: /mine/` and a single service worker at the root. Subfolders are ordinary pages
inside that scope, reached by navigation.

This is what makes "set the token once" work: `/mine/` and `/mine/calendar/` are the
same origin, so they share one IndexedDB automatically, with no message passing. If each
folder were installed as its own home-screen app, iOS would give each one an isolated
storage container and the token would have to be entered again per app.

### Layout

```
/index.html            tile screen
/manifest.json         scope and start_url: /mine/
/sw.js                 one service worker, root scope, type: module
/shared/
  apps.js              APPS list - single source of truth
  store.js             IndexedDB: settings + file cache + sync queue
  github.js            GitHub API: bootstrap, pull, drain
  md.js                frontmatter parse / serialize
  vendor/              pinned third-party code, see VENDOR.md
/calendar/
  index.html
  app.js               imports ../shared/*.js by relative path
  widget.js            optional, exports summary()
  icon.svg
  REQUIREMENTS.md
  sample/
```

No build step. No bundler, no node_modules, no CI. `git push` is the deploy, and every
page can be opened directly from disk. All paths are relative, so the `/mine/` prefix
needs no configuration.

### Tile screen

`shared/apps.js` exports the list of apps and is imported by both the tile screen and
the service worker's precache list, so adding an app means editing one array.

Each tile shows the app's `icon.svg` above its folder name. An app may additionally ship
a `widget.js` exporting `summary()`; whatever it returns is rendered above the tiles.
The calendar's widget shows today's entries and the next one. This is deliberate: see
*Alerts* below — opening the app is the only reminder mechanism that works.

## PWA Setup & GitHub Sync

### Initialization (first run)

- User opens the main app URL (GitHub Pages) on the phone.
- User installs it via "Add to Home Screen" (iOS: Safari -> Share; Android: Chrome menu).
- On first launch, the app shows a setup screen asking for:
  - GitHub owner, **data** repo, and branch
  - Fine-grained personal access token, scoped to that one repo, "Contents: read and
    write", with an expiry date
- App checks the connection with a test request (`GET /repos/{owner}/{repo}`); on failure
  it shows a clear error naming the failing step.
- Settings and token are stored in IndexedDB. The expiry date is stored alongside, and
  the app warns 14 days before the token lapses. The token is never logged or displayed
  after entry.
- Service worker caches the app shell so the app opens offline.

### Token handling

The token is stored in plaintext in IndexedDB: it is as safe as the unlocked device. The
threat that matters is not a stolen phone but injected script on our own origin, which is
closed off by policy rather than encryption:

- Every page sends a strict CSP:
  `default-src 'self'; script-src 'self'; connect-src 'self' https://api.github.com https://codeload.github.com`
- **No CDNs, ever.** Every dependency is committed to `/shared/vendor/` and pinned by
  hand, with its source URL and version recorded in `VENDOR.md`. No unpkg, no cdnjs,
  no Google Fonts.
- The token is never written to a log, a URL, or the DOM.

### Cache model

Each app folder is mirrored locally in full. A decade of calendar entries is roughly
3000 files of ~500 B, so mirroring costs less than range-tracking logic and makes every
date available offline and search local and instant.

**Bootstrap** (first open of an app, 2 requests):

1. `GET /repos/{o}/{r}/tarball/{branch}` — the whole tree in one request. Decompressed
   with the native `DecompressionStream('gzip')`; the tar walk is ~40 lines.
2. `GET /repos/{o}/{r}/git/trees/{branch}?recursive=1` — all paths with their blob SHAs.

Only the opened app's folder is kept. Blob SHAs are stored per path; they are what later
pulls diff against and what writes send as their expected base.

**Pull** (on app open and on window focus):

1. `GET /repos/{o}/{r}/commits/{branch}` with `If-None-Match`. A `304` means nothing
   changed and costs no rate-limit quota.
2. On `200`: fetch the tree, diff blob SHAs against the cache, and fetch only the files
   whose SHA changed. Deleted paths are dropped from the cache.

### Sending data to GitHub

- User creates, edits, moves or deletes an item.
- The change is written to the local cache immediately (UI updates instantly) and appended
  to a sync queue. Each queued change records the blob SHA it was based on.
- The sync worker drains the whole queue as **one atomic commit** via the Git Data API:
  - `POST /git/blobs` per changed file
  - `POST /git/trees` with `base_tree` set to the current tree, listing additions and
    deletions (a deletion is an entry with `sha: null`)
  - `POST /git/commits`
  - `PATCH /git/refs/heads/{branch}` with the expected old SHA and **no force**
- One drain is one commit, so moving an entry — a delete plus a create, because the date
  is part of the path and the API has no rename — can never be half-applied, and a
  20-item offline backlog is one commit rather than twenty.
- If the ref update is rejected, someone pushed from elsewhere: pull, rebuild the tree on
  the new base, and retry. This succeeds, because almost every write in Mine is a create
  at a freshly generated path and cannot collide.
- **True conflict** — a queued change whose recorded base SHA no longer matches the remote
  blob at that path — means the same entry was edited in two places. Nothing is discarded:
  the remote version keeps the canonical path, and the local version is committed beside it
  as `<name>.conflict-<yyyymmdd>.md` with a `conflictOf:` key naming the original. The UI
  shows a banner offering keep mine / keep theirs / keep both. The leftover is plain
  markdown, readable in any editor and visible on every device. The queue never jams.
- On 401/403: pause sync and link the user to settings to renew the token.
- Offline: the queue persists in IndexedDB and drains automatically when connectivity
  returns or the app is reopened.
- A sync indicator shows: in sync / pending / error.

Note that GitHub's Background Sync API does not exist in Safari, so draining happens in
the foreground, whenever the app is open.

### Service worker

- One service worker at the root, registered with `{type: 'module'}` so it can import the
  same `shared/apps.js` the tile screen uses.
- A version constant names the cache. On install the shell is precached: every page,
  every `shared/` module, `vendor/`, the icons and the manifest.
- Same-origin requests are served from cache and revalidated in the background.
- Requests to `api.github.com` and `codeload.github.com` **bypass the service worker
  entirely**. Caching an API response would hand back a stale ETag and silently break
  sync.
- A new service worker waits rather than activating. The UI shows an "Update ready —
  reload" banner, and `skipWaiting()` runs only on the user's tap, so an upgrade never
  lands mid-edit.

### Alerts

**No browser can schedule a local notification for a time when the app is closed.** The
Notification Triggers API was an origin trial that never shipped, and Periodic Background
Sync does not exist in Safari. Web Push would work, but something must be awake to send
it, which means a scheduler holding a token off-device.

For this reason, in v1:

- `alerts:` is stored and exported (it is valid `VALARM` data for `.ics`), but nothing
  fires in the background. Mine will not remind you while it is closed, and the
  requirements say so rather than implying otherwise.
- While the app is open, due alerts fire as real `Notification`s via `setTimeout`.
- The tile screen's calendar widget shows today and what is next, so opening the app is
  the reminder.

If background reminders are wanted later, the cheapest path that keeps data in these two
repos is a scheduled GitHub Actions workflow in the data repo sending Web Push with VAPID
keys held as repo secrets — accepting that GitHub cron drifts 5–20 minutes.

### Dependencies

Vendored into `/shared/vendor/`, pinned by hand:

| What | Why not hand-rolled |
| --- | --- |
| `js-yaml` | Files are hand-edited in an editor and must parse as real YAML — quoting, multiline scalars, flow maps. A subset parser misreads them silently. |
| `rrule` | `FREQ=MONTHLY;BYDAY=-1FR` and DST-crossing weeklies are where hand-rolled expansion is wrong without telling you. |

YAML *writing* is ours (~20 lines): we control the output shape, so no dumper is needed.

## Spikes — unverified assumptions

Each of these is cheap to test and each has a documented fallback. They should be proven
on the actual target device before the code depending on them grows.

1. **codeload CORS.** `GET /tarball/{ref}` 302-redirects to `codeload.github.com`. If
   that host does not send `Access-Control-Allow-Origin` for an authenticated private-repo
   download, the browser fetch fails after the redirect.
   *Fallback:* bootstrap by walking the tree and fetching each blob individually — fine
   at today's file counts, degrading over the years.
2. **iOS shared storage.** That an installed PWA at `/mine/` really does share one
   IndexedDB with `/mine/calendar/` on the target iOS version.
   *Fallback:* none that is pleasant — this assumption is load-bearing for the whole
   "set the token once" design, so test it first.
3. **Module service workers.** `{type: 'module'}` requires Safari 16.4+.
   *Fallback:* a classic service worker with the app list duplicated in `sw.js`.
EOF

# Calendar

Calendar is an app of [Mine](../REQUIREMENTS.md) to manage your calendar. It stores one
entry per markdown file in the data repo and holds no state of its own beyond the shared
cache described in the root requirements.

## Data model

### Paths

```
calendar/2026/04/2026-04-18-1400-k3f9.md     one-off entry
calendar/2026/04/2026-04-25-0000-ov1q.md     occurrence override
calendar/recurring/trash-p7qm.md             entry with a recurrence rule
calendar/groups.md                           group -> colour mapping
```

The date lives in the path, so the Trees API listing alone tells the app which days have
entries, before any file content is downloaded. The `-k3f9` suffix is 4 random characters,
**not** a counter: two devices creating entries offline on the same day must never mint
the same name. No title slug is used, so editing a title is never a rename.

Entries carrying a `recurrence:` rule live in `calendar/recurring/` instead of the date
tree, because an open-ended rule must render in months it was not created in. That folder
stays small (tens of files) and is always cached; a view is that month's folder plus every
rule expanded in memory over the visible range.

### Frontmatter

Keys follow RFC 5545 (iCalendar) naming where one exists, so `.ics` export is close to a
field copy. **Empty keys are omitted, never written as `None`** — `None` is a YAML string,
not null, and a parser hands it back as the text `"None"`.

| Key | Applies to | Notes |
| --- | --- | --- |
| `title` | both | required |
| `type` | both | `event` or `task` |
| `start` | both | `DTSTART`. A bare date (`2026-04-18`) is all-day; a timestamp (`2026-04-18T14:00:00Z`) is an instant |
| `end` | both | same value types as `start`; omitted for all-day single-day items |
| `group` | both | a name, resolved through `groups.md` |
| `done` | `task` only | `true` / `false` |
| `location` | both | free text |
| `alerts` | both | list of minutes before start; `0` means at start. Stored and exported only — see *Alerts* in the root requirements |
| `participants` | both | list of email addresses |
| `recurrence` | both | an RFC 5545 RRULE string, e.g. `FREQ=WEEKLY;BYDAY=SA` |
| `exdate` | recurring | occurrences to skip |
| `rdate` | recurring | extra occurrences outside the rule |
| `series` | override | the id of the recurring file it belongs to |
| `recurrence-id` | override | `RECURRENCE-ID`: the original occurrence date this file replaces |
| `conflictOf` | conflict file | written by sync, see root requirements |

There is no `duration` key — it is `end - start`.

The bare-date form matters: storing an all-day task as `2026-04-18T00:00:00Z` puts it on
the wrong day for anyone not on UTC, and breaks twice a year on DST.

The markdown body below the frontmatter is the entry's content — an agenda, a checklist,
notes. It is preserved byte-for-byte by anything that does not explicitly edit it.

### Recurrence and per-occurrence state

A recurring file states the rule only. Anything that happens to a *single* occurrence —
ticking it done, moving it, retitling it, cancelling it — is written as an **override
file** in the date tree carrying `series:` and `recurrence-id:`. The rule file is never
rewritten, and because each override is a fresh path it can never conflict, even when
created offline on two devices.

When rendering, an expanded occurrence is replaced by any override whose `recurrence-id`
matches its date. `exdate:` remains available for a plain skip with nothing to record.

Full RRULE is supported on read, since files may be hand-written or imported. The UI only
*writes* the common cases: daily / weekly / monthly / yearly, `INTERVAL`, `BYDAY`,
`UNTIL`, `COUNT`.

### Groups

An entry's `group` is a semantic name, not a colour. `calendar/groups.md` maps it to a
colour and a label, so recolouring or relabelling a group is a one-file edit rather than a
rewrite of every entry that used it, and there is no cap on the number of groups. An
unknown group renders grey. The file lives in the data repo, so the mapping follows you
across devices.

## UI

The UI consists of a navigation pane at the top and a big calendar window on the rest of
the window.

In the top pane are these widgets from left to right:

- left/right button to move to the previous/next day/week/month/year (depending on current view)
- the current day/week/month/year with a small downward arrow to indicate a dropdown. When
  clicked a calendar month view is shown with all days in this dropdown view. The month is
  shown on the top left and on the top right is a left/right arrow to go to the
  previous/next month. When the user clicks on the month in the extended view it switches
  to year. The year view shows 9 years in a 3x3 grid ending with the current year, and its
  left/right arrows page back and forward by 9 years.
- A dropdown to select the view to be either day/week/month/year.
- A dropdown to filter the calendar groups by colour. Double-clicking a group icon lets the
  user edit its label; this writes `groups.md`.

All views show **7 columns, Monday through Sunday**. Weekend columns are tinted so the
work week still reads as a block. (The data requires this: a `BYDAY=SA` task is invisible
in a five-column view.)

- The **year view** shows all months and days. On the top of each month is a
  `['M','T','W','T','F','S','S']` row indicating the weekday. Each row is a new week. The
  current day is highlighted. The user can click a day and a popup shows the entries on
  that day. If there is a calendar entry on that day the day has the background colour of
  the entry's group. For multiple entries the background is split. A group disabled in the
  filter dropdown is not shown.
- The **month view** rows are weeks. Entries appear as rows inside each day cell, sorted by
  start time. `task` items have a rectangular icon at the right to mark them done; a
  completed item shows a check in the rectangle. A task has only a date, no time.
- The **week view** columns are the days, rows are the 24 hours of the day.
- The **day view** is the week view for a single day, showing more detail per entry.

### Entry popup

A top row for the title; below it a button group to select the type; below that the
remaining fields (see `sample/`); below those an auto-growing monospace textarea holding
the markdown body as raw text. At the bottom are a `discard` and a `save` button.

The body is edited and displayed as raw markdown — no renderer, so what you see is exactly
what lands in the file, and there is no third dependency to sanitise HTML for.

### Phone layout

The views above describe the desktop layout. The phone is the primary install target and
a month cell there is ~50px wide, so entry rows are neither readable nor tappable. The
same files adapt at a CSS breakpoint:

- The top pane collapses to `[<] [April 2026 v] [=]`.
- Month and year cells show group-coloured dots instead of text rows.
- Tapping a day opens a bottom sheet listing that day's entries, each tappable to edit,
  with a `+ add entry` button — so no tap target is ever smaller than a finger.
- On desktop, clicking empty space in a day cell creates an entry and clicking an entry
  row opens it.

### Widget

`widget.js` exports `summary()`, returning today's entries and the next upcoming one for
the tile screen of the main app.

lines: # Calendar
- # Calendar
-Calendar is a plugin to manage your calendar.
+Calendar is an app of [Mine](../REQUIREMENTS.md) to manage your calendar. It stores one
+entry per markdown file in the data repo and holds no state of its own beyond the shared
+cache described in the root requirements.
-Features
+## Data model
+### Paths
+calendar/2026/04/2026-04-18-1400-k3f9.md     one-off entry
+calendar/2026/04/2026-04-25-0000-ov1q.md     occurrence override
+calendar/recurring/trash-p7qm.md             entry with a recurrence rule
+calendar/groups.md                           group -> colour mapping
+The date lives in the path, so the Trees API listing alone tells the app which days have
+entries, before any file content is downloaded. The `-k3f9` suffix is 4 random characters,
+**not** a counter: two devices creating entries offline on the same day must never mint
+the same name. No title slug is used, so editing a title is never a rename.
+Entries carrying a `recurrence:` rule live in `calendar/recurring/` instead of the date
+tree, because an open-ended rule must render in months it was not created in. That folder
+stays small (tens of files) and is always cached; a view is that month's folder plus every
+rule expanded in memory over the visible range.
+### Frontmatter
+Keys follow RFC 5545 (iCalendar) naming where one exists, so `.ics` export is close to a
+field copy. **Empty keys are omitted, never written as `None`** — `None` is a YAML string,
+not null, and a parser hands it back as the text `"None"`.
+| Key | Applies to | Notes |
+| `title` | both | required |
+| `type` | both | `event` or `task` |
+| `start` | both | `DTSTART`. A bare date (`2026-04-18`) is all-day; a timestamp (`2026-04-18T14:00:00Z`) is an instant |
+| `end` | both | same value types as `start`; omitted for all-day single-day items |
+| `group` | both | a name, resolved through `groups.md` |
+| `done` | `task` only | `true` / `false` |
+| `location` | both | free text |
+| `alerts` | both | list of minutes before start; `0` means at start. Stored and exported only — see *Alerts* in the root requirements |
+| `participants` | both | list of email addresses |
+| `recurrence` | both | an RFC 5545 RRULE string, e.g. `FREQ=WEEKLY;BYDAY=SA` |
+| `exdate` | recurring | occurrences to skip |
+| `rdate` | recurring | extra occurrences outside the rule |
+| `series` | override | the id of the recurring file it belongs to |
+| `recurrence-id` | override | `RECURRENCE-ID`: the original occurrence date this file replaces |
+| `conflictOf` | conflict file | written by sync, see root requirements |
+There is no `duration` key — it is `end - start`.
+The bare-date form matters: storing an all-day task as `2026-04-18T00:00:00Z` puts it on
+the wrong day for anyone not on UTC, and breaks twice a year on DST.
+The markdown body below the frontmatter is the entry's content — an agenda, a checklist,
+notes. It is preserved byte-for-byte by anything that does not explicitly edit it.
+### Recurrence and per-occurrence state
+A recurring file states the rule only. Anything that happens to a *single* occurrence —
+ticking it done, moving it, retitling it, cancelling it — is written as an **override
+file** in the date tree carrying `series:` and `recurrence-id:`. The rule file is never
+rewritten, and because each override is a fresh path it can never conflict, even when
+created offline on two devices.
+When rendering, an expanded occurrence is replaced by any override whose `recurrence-id`
+matches its date. `exdate:` remains available for a plain skip with nothing to record.
+Full RRULE is supported on read, since files may be hand-written or imported. The UI only
+*writes* the common cases: daily / weekly / monthly / yearly, `INTERVAL`, `BYDAY`,
+`UNTIL`, `COUNT`.
+### Groups
+An entry's `group` is a semantic name, not a colour. `calendar/groups.md` maps it to a
+colour and a label, so recolouring or relabelling a group is a one-file edit rather than a
+rewrite of every entry that used it, and there is no cap on the number of groups. An
+unknown group renders grey. The file lives in the data repo, so the mapping follows you
+across devices.
## UI
-- The UI consists of a navigation pane at the top and a big calendar window on the rest of the window.
-- In the top pane are these widgets from left to right:
-  - left/right button to move to the previous/next day/week/month/year (depending on current view)

-  - the current day/week/month/year with a small downward arrow to indicate a dropdown. When clicked a calendar month view is show with all days in this dropdown view. The month is shown on the top left and on the top right is a left/right arrow to go to the previous/next month.  When the user clicks on the month in the extended view it switches to year. -    - The year view shows all months and days. On the top of each month is a ['M','T','W','T','F','S','S'] column indicating the weekday. Each row is a new week. Current day is highlighted. content.text:
Both requirements files are rewritten and the samples now mirror the real data-repo layout. Nothing committed — that's yours.

**Answers to your two questions:**

Yes, the shared token works — and for a boring reason that's worth knowing: `/mine/` and `/mine/calendar/` are one origin, so one IndexedDB, no plumbing. The condition is that it stays **one installed PWA** with folders as routes. Install the calendar separately and iOS isolates its storage.

The REQUIREMENTS mostly made sense — the sync chapter was the right shape already. Seven things were wrong or missing, all now fixed:

| Was | Now |
| --- | --- |
| No repo split | public `mine` (Pages) + private `mine-data`; token scoped to data only |
| `alerts` implied working reminders | stated plainly: **nothing fires while closed**, no API exists; widget on the tile screen is the reminder |
| Samples disagreed (`start:`/`date:`, `done: None`) | one schema, RFC 5545 naming, `None` banned, bare date = all-day |
| `repeat: weekly` unanswerable | your `recurrence:` RRULE, in `recurring/`, with override files per occurrence |
| `20260418-1.md` counter | 4 random chars — two offline devices can't collide |
| Conflict = discard your edit | remote keeps the path, yours lands beside it as `.conflict-*.md` |
| Contents API, non-atomic moves | Git Data API, one commit per drain |

Three things I changed my mind on while costing them out, so you don't inherit my first answer: the "fetch *all* markdown" clause you wrote was right and my lazy-loading objection was wrong (1.5 MB after a decade); the tarball bootstrap replaces 3000 requests with 1; and your `BYDAY=SA` trash task is what settles "workdays" → 7 columns.

**Before writing code, three assumptions need 20 minutes on your actual phone** — documented as spikes with fallbacks at the end of `REQUIREMENTS.md`. The load-bearing one is #2: if an installed iOS PWA doesn't share IndexedDB across `/mine/calendar/`, the premise of your whole question fails and there's no pleasant fallback. #1 (does `codeload.github.com` send CORS headers for authenticated private downloads?) I genuinely don't know — it only costs you the tarball optimisation.

content.text:
Spike #1 is settled, and the answer is **no** — the tarball bootstrap is dead:

```
api.github.com/tarball  →  302  access-control-allow-origin: *
codeload.github.com     →  200  access-control-allow-origin: https://render.githubusercontent.com
OPTIONS preflight       →  403
```

`fetch()` follows the redirect automatically and then applies the CORS check to the *final* response. codeload names one specific foreign origin, so the browser blocks the read — and since an authenticated request needs a preflight, which 403s, it fails twice over. No phone needed; that one's conclusive.

Also: neither `adb` nor `libimobiledevice` is installed here, so "connected" doesn't give me a shell on either device. That's fine — installing a PWA to the home screen is UI-only anyway, so spike #2 was always going to be you tapping. Let me first see whether the fallback is as bad as I documented, because one request per file is a grim bootstrap:

GraphQL changes the picture completely. The fallback I documented (one request per file) isn't needed:

- `access-control-allow-origin: *` and a 204 preflight that explicitly allows `Authorization` → **browser-usable**, unlike codeload.
- A nested `Tree`/`Blob` query returns a whole folder tree *with file contents* in one response.
- `rateLimit.cost: 1` — one point, regardless of how many files come back, because `entries` isn't a paginated connection.

content.text: `oid` is byte-identical to the REST tree SHA (`980a0d5f…`), so **one** GraphQL query yields paths, contents and SHAs together. Bootstrap drops from 2 requests to 1. Updating the docs:

input.command:
python3 -I - <<'PY'
import re
p = 'REQUIREMENTS.md'
s = open(p).read()

old_boot = s[s.index('**Bootstrap** (first open of an app, 2 requests):'):s.index('**Pull** (on app open and on window focus):')]
new_boot = '''**Bootstrap** (first open of an app, **1 request**):

A single GraphQL query returns the app's folder tree *with file contents and blob SHAs*,
nested to the depth of the layout (`calendar` -> year -> month -> blob):

```graphql
repository(owner:$o, name:$r) {
  object(expression: "main:calendar") {
    ... on Tree { entries { name type
      object { ... on Tree { entries { name type
        object { ... on Tree { entries { name type
          object { ... on Blob { oid text isTruncated } } } } } } } } } }
}
```

Verified against the live API: `rateLimit.cost` is **1** regardless of how many files come
back, because `entries` is not a paginated connection; a 16 MB / 145 file response returned
without error in 6 s. `Blob.oid` is byte-identical to the REST tree SHA, so this one request
also supplies the SHAs that pulls diff against and writes send as their base.

`isTruncated` must be checked: GraphQL truncates very large blobs and returns `text: null`
for binary. Markdown entries are far below the limit, but a truncated blob falls back to a
REST blob fetch for that one path.

'''
s = s.replace(old_boot, new_boot)

# codeload is no longer contacted at all
s = s.replace("`default-src 'self'; script-src 'self'; connect-src 'self' https://api.github.com https://codeload.github.com`",
              "`default-src 'self'; script-src 'self'; connect-src 'self' https://api.github.com`")
s = s.replace("""- Requests to `api.github.com` and `codeload.github.com` **bypass the service worker
  entirely**.""",
              """- Requests to `api.github.com` **bypass the service worker entirely**.""")

old_spikes = s[s.index('## Spikes — unverified assumptions'):]
new_spikes = '''## Verified facts

Tested against the live API on 2026-11-19; see `/spike/` for the on-device page.

- **The tarball bootstrap is impossible from a browser.** `GET /tarball/{ref}` 302-redirects
  to `codeload.github.com`, which answers `access-control-allow-origin:
  https://render.githubusercontent.com` — one specific foreign origin, not ours and not `*`.
  `fetch()` applies the CORS check to the final response after following the redirect, so the
  read is blocked; the `OPTIONS` preflight an authenticated request would need returns 403.
- **GraphQL replaces it and is better.** `api.github.com/graphql` sends
  `access-control-allow-origin: *` and a 204 preflight explicitly allowing `Authorization`,
  so it is browser-usable. One query, cost 1, contents and SHAs together.

## Open spikes — on-device assumptions

`/spike/` is a token-free page that tests all of these on a real phone. Each needs a
documented fallback before code depends on it.

1. **Shared storage across paths in an installed PWA.** That a value written by `/mine/`
   is readable by `/mine/calendar/` once the app is launched from the home screen. This is
   load-bearing for the entire "set the token once" design, so it is tested first.
   *Fallback:* none that is pleasant. If it fails, each app folder needs its own token
   entry, or the apps must become one page with client-side routing.
2. **Module service workers.** `{type: 'module'}` requires Safari 16.4+, and is what lets
   `sw.js` import the same `shared/apps.js` the tile screen uses.
   *Fallback:* a classic service worker with the app list duplicated in `sw.js`. The spike
   page attempts the classic registration automatically if the module one fails.
3. **Storage persistence.** iOS evicts script-writable storage after roughly seven days
   without engagement unless the site is installed. If `navigator.storage.persist()` is not
   granted, the token and the whole local mirror can vanish between uses.
   *Fallback:* treat the cache as disposable and re-bootstrap on launch — cheap now that
   bootstrap is one request — but the **token** disappearing means re-entering it, which
   would make a short-expiry token-per-device policy mandatory rather than optional.

is one atomic commit, and conflicts preserved as sibling files instead of
discarding local edits.

browser because codeload.github.com restricts CORS to one foreign origin,
while GraphQL allows any origin and returns contents plus blob SHAs for a
rate-limit cost of 1.

Co-Authored-By: Claude Opus 5 <noreply@anthropic.com>
EOF

content.text:
Live: **https://maximilianharr.github.io/mine/spike/** — all subresources serving with correct MIME types (`sw.js` as `application/javascript`, which Pages sometimes gets wrong and which silently breaks SW registration).

Everything from here is physical taps; I can't drive either device. Order matters on the iPhone.

**iPhone — must be Safari** (Chrome on iOS can't create a real PWA):

1. Open the URL in Safari → tap **Write marker here**
2. Share → **Add to Home Screen** → Add
3. Launch **Spike** from the home screen
4. Confirm `launched as` says **STANDALONE** — if it says "browser tab", the install didn't take and nothing below is meaningful
5. The marker row will probably say **EMPTY** here. **That is expected, not a failure** — iOS gives an installed app a storage container separate from Safari's. So tap **Write marker here** again, now inside the installed app
6. Tap **Go to /sub/**

**Pixel — Chrome:** same sequence, step 2 is menu → **Install app**.

The verdict is one row on the `/sub/` page:

| `IndexedDB marker visible here` | Meaning |
|---|---|
| ✓ with `written at /mine/spike/ (STANDALONE…)` | Shared-token design holds. Build as specified. |
| ✗ EMPTY while STANDALONE | Open spike #1 fails — each folder would need its own token, or the folders must collapse into one client-routed page. |

Four other rows worth reading back to me, in both the root and `/sub/` summaries:

- `service worker {type:module}` — open spike #2; root page only. A ✗ here just means `sw.js` duplicates the app list.
- `storage persisted (not evictable)` — open spike #3, and the one I'd most expect to misbehave on iOS. A ✗ means your token can be evicted after ~7 days idle.
- `GraphQL reachable from browser` — expects `HTTP 401/403 readable`; that's a **pass**, since an unauthenticated query is supposed to be rejected. What's being tested is that CORS let the response through at all.
- `tarball blocked (expected FAIL=good)` — a ✓ confirms on-device what curl showed.

Paste or screenshot the grey summary block from each page and I'll fold the results into the requirements — including deleting `spike/` once the three are settled.

content.text:
A "spike" is throwaway test code. Not part of the app — its only job is to answer a question I couldn't answer from docs, before we build anything on top of a guess.

I had three guesses that the whole design rests on. `spike/` is one tiny page that just checks them on your actual phones:

1. If you type the token at `/mine/`, can `/mine/calendar/` read it once the app is installed? (If no, your "set it once" idea doesn't work.)
2. Does your iPhone's Safari support the newer service worker style?
3. Will iOS throw the token away after a week of not using the app?

The page writes a marker, you install it, open the subfolder, and it shows you ✓ or ✗ for each. That's all.

Then it gets deleted. It's scaffolding — cheaper to write 100 throwaway lines now than to build the whole calendar and discover assumption 1 was wrong.

All five screenshots are the **root** page (`page: /mine/spike/`) — on both devices. That closes two of the three spikes outright, but the load-bearing one is still untested: the root page reading back its own marker proves nothing about path sharing, since the same path wrote it.

**Closed, both devices:**

| | Pixel / Chrome | iPhone / Safari |
|---|---|---|
| launched as | STANDALONE | STANDALONE |
| service worker `{type:module}` | registered | registered |
| storage persisted | already granted | already granted |
| GraphQL CORS | 403 readable ✓ | 403 readable ✓ |
| tarball | blocked (NetworkError) | blocked (Load failed) |
| quota | 56 GB | 35 GB |

Two of those are better news than I expected. Module SW works on Safari, so `sw.js` can import the same `shared/apps.js` — no duplicated app list. And `persisted()` was **already granted** without a prompt on iOS, which means the token and mirror are exempt from the 7-day eviction I warned about. Recording that:

  "NetworkError" on Chrome — inside both installed apps.

'''

Pushed as `7ecb967`. Both your original questions are now answered with evidence rather than my judgement:

**Is it possible?** Yes, verified on your actual hardware. Token entered once at `/mine/`, readable from `/mine/calendar/`, in the installed app on both phones.

**Did the REQUIREMENTS make sense?** The sync architecture did. Nine things didn't, and are fixed. Three of those were things neither of us could have known without testing — and two went the opposite way from my predictions:

- I warned iOS might evict your token after ~7 days idle. It won't: `persisted()` was **already granted**, no prompt.
- I warned module service workers might not work on Safari. They do, so `sw.js` imports the same app list as the tile screen instead of duplicating it.
- I documented a tarball bootstrap. It's impossible from a browser — codeload restricts CORS to one foreign origin. GraphQL replaced it and is better than what I originally specified: 1 request instead of 2, contents *and* SHAs together, rate-limit cost 1.

Untested and documented as such: whether separately-installed PWAs really do get isolated storage. It's the reason we didn't take that path, and it no longer matters.

**Before any app code, two things are yours to do** — I can't mint a token on your behalf:

1. Create the private `mine-data` repo (I can run this if you want: `gh repo create maximilianharr/mine-data --private`)
2. Mint a fine-grained PAT scoped to it, Contents: read and write, with an expiry

Then the build order I'd suggest is `shared/` first — `store.js`, `github.js`, `md.js` — proven end-to-end by a settings screen that writes one real file to `mine-data`, before any calendar UI exists. That's the smallest thing that proves the architecture works with a real token against a real repo.
